content.title: About
content.content: Fajita is a Mexican dish consisting of thinly sliced beef or pork quickly seared on high heat with onions, bell peppers, and spices. The meat stays juicy while the vegetables become aromatic and slightly charred. It is usually served with tortillas, salsa, guacamole, and sour cream.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The word “fajita” comes from the Spanish “faja,” meaning “strip,” originally referring to strips of skirt steak.
Traditionally fajitas were made with skirt steak, but today pork, chicken, and even seafood are common alternatives.
The dish gained popularity in the United States in the 1970s thanks to the Taco Bell chain.
Authentic flavor often includes cumin, paprika, oregano, chili powder, and lime juice.
Fajitas are typically served “build‑your‑own,” letting each guest assemble the tortilla to taste.

items.title: Rich source of protein
items.content: Beef and pork provide high‑quality protein essential for muscle growth and tissue repair.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: The meat is abundant in B12, niacin, and riboflavin, supporting energy metabolism and nervous system health.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: Fajita supplies iron, zinc, and phosphorus, important for blood formation, immunity, and bone health.

items.title: Low in carbohydrates
items.content: When served without sugary sauces, fajitas fit well into low‑carb diets.

items.title: Antioxidants from vegetables
items.content: Onions and bell peppers add vitamin C and carotenoids that help protect cells.

items.title: Saturated fat content
items.content: Pork and beef can contain saturated fats; choosing lean cuts and moderate portions is advisable.

items.title: Risk of over‑eating
items.content: The dish is often accompanied by tortillas and sauces, which can increase total calories if consumed in large amounts.

items.title: Spice allergy
items.content: Some individuals may be sensitive to chili, cumin, or other spices used in the marinade.

items.title: Food‑borne contamination
items.content: Meat must be fully cooked to avoid bacterial infections.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve fajita in warm tortillas, adding salsa, guacamole, sour cream, shredded cheese, and fresh cilantro. It can also be used as a filling for burritos, tacos, or salads.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep raw meat in the refrigerator for up to 2 days; cooked fajita can be stored in an airtight container for up to 3 days. For longer storage, freeze in bags for up to 3 months. Thaw in the fridge and reheat on a skillet before serving.
